title: Cap. X Arg. IX: from the nature of negative non-election — reprobation is denied placing of undue grace, not imposition of punishment; Rom. ix. 15
latin: A natura non-electionis sive reprobationis negativae ita possumus argumentari; haec reprobatio formaliter considerata non est impositio poenae, sed negata appositio indebitae gratiae. Ac tale beneficium negare vel concedere pertinet ad absolutam Dei potestatem, juxta illud Apostoli ex Mose petitum, Miserebor cujus misertus fuero, et commiserabor quem commiseratus fuero, Rom. ix. 15.
pass_a: From the nature of non-election or negative reprobation we can thus argue; this reprobation formally considered is not the imposition of a penalty, but the denied placing of undue grace. And to deny or to grant such a benefit pertains unto the absolute power of God, according to that of the Apostle taken from Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have had mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have had compassion, Rom. ix. 15.
pass_b: From the nature of non-election—negative reprobation—we argue thus: formally considered, this reprobation is not laying on a penalty, but refusing to place grace that was never owed. To deny or grant such a benefit belongs to God’s absolute power, after the Apostle’s word from Moses (Rom. ix. 15): I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.

lemmas.lemma: non est impositio poenae, sed negata appositio

title: Cap. X Arg. IX: reprobation not a punishment — shown in reprobate angels whom Suarez, Bellarmine, Vasquez say God passed by with no merited penalty in them
latin: Reprobationem autem sive non-electionem non esse poenam; quamvis reprobati semper in poenas incidant sempiternas, patet exemplo Angelorum reprobatorum, sive non-electorum, in quibus nihil erat quod poenam sive supplicium mereretur, et tamen Deus quosdam ex illis elegit, alios non elegit sed praeteriit, fatente Suarez, Bellarmino, Vasquez, ac consentientibus omnibus Theologis.
pass_a: But that reprobation or non-election is not a penalty—although the reprobate always fall into everlasting penalties—is plain from the example of the reprobate, or non-elect, Angels, in whom there was nothing that deserved a penalty or torment, and yet God elected certain of them, others he did not elect but passed by, Suarez, Bellarmine, Vasquez confessing it, and all Theologians agreeing.
pass_b: That reprobation or non-election is not itself a penalty—though the reprobate always fall into everlasting pains—is plain from the reprobate or non-elect angels: in them there was nothing that deserved penalty or torment, yet God chose some and passed others by. Suarez, Bellarmine, and Vasquez confess it, and the theologians agree.

title: Cap. X Arg. IX: they add God’s will as cause of angelic non-election with no cause expected from the non-elect; before any foreseen demonic sin (Suarez, Vasquez, Bellarmine)
latin: Neque id solum dicunt, Deum absoluta et antecedente voluntate quosdam ex hisce Angelis elegisse, quosdam praeteriisse, sed addunt expresse, solam Dei voluntatem esse causam hujus non-electionis, nulla exspectata causa ex parte non-electorum: Sic Suarez Opusc. pag. 175. Dicunt, Hanc reprobationem factam ante omne peccatum praevisum in ipsis daemonibus: Sic Vasquez in 1. pag. 698, et 701. Docent denique et probant, Hanc reprobationem non pependisse ex praevisione peccati in iisdem: Sic Bellarminus, De grat. et lib. arbitr. lib. 2. cap. 17.
pass_a: Nor do they say that alone, that God by absolute and antecedent will elected certain of these Angels, passed by certain; but they add expressly that God’s will alone is the cause of this non-election, no cause being expected from the part of the non-elect: Thus Suarez Opusc. pag. 175. They say, This reprobation was made before every sin foreseen in the demons themselves: Thus Vasquez in 1. pag. 698, and 701. Finally they teach and prove that This reprobation did not hang from foresight of sin in the same: Thus Bellarmine, De grat. et lib. arbitr. lib. 2. cap. 17.
pass_b: They say more: God by absolute antecedent will chose some angels and passed others by—and they add expressly that God’s will alone is the cause of that non-election, with no cause looked for on the non-elect’s side. So Suarez (Opusc. p. 175): this reprobation was made before any sin foreseen in the demons. So Vasquez (in 1, pp. 698, 701). And they teach and prove that this reprobation did not hang on foresight of sin in them—so Bellarmine (De gratia et libero arbitrio 2.17).

title: Cap. X Arg. IX: objection — angelic preterition is mere denial of undue benefit, but human reprobation is true punishment from foreseen unbelief — refuted by distinguishing decrees about the fallen
latin: Quod si quis obtendat, In Angelis quidem hanc reprobationem non habuisse rationem supplicii, sed fuisse nudam negationem indebiti beneficii, atque idcirco haud requirere antecedaneam praevisionem rebellionis tanquam causam ejus motivam, in hominibus autem esse veram et proprie dictam poenam, atque eapropter ex praevisione infidelitatis et perseverantiae in eadem necessario arcessendam, id facile refellitur. Nam circa hominem lapsum et peccatis constrictum, atque tandem propter peccata puniendum, decreta divinae voluntatis diversa, et sub diversis respectibus possunt et debent considerari.
pass_a: But if anyone object that In the Angels indeed this reprobation did not have the character of torment, but was a bare negation of an undue benefit, and therefore by no means requires antecedent foresight of rebellion as its motive cause, yet in men it is a true and properly so called penalty, and for that reason must necessarily be fetched from foresight of unbelief and of perseverance in the same—that is easily refuted. For concerning man fallen and bound with sins, and at length to be punished for sins, the decrees of the divine will are diverse, and under diverse respects can and ought to be considered.
pass_b: If someone objects that in angels this reprobation was not torment but bare denial of an unowed benefit—and so needs no antecedent foresight of rebellion as its motive—yet in men it is true punishment properly so called, and must therefore be fetched from foresight of unbelief and perseverance in it: that is easily answered. About fallen man, bound in sins and at last to be punished for them, the decrees of the divine will are diverse and must be weighed under diverse respects.

lemmas.gloss: objection: angels = bare denial of benefit

title: Cap. X Arg. IX: Judas — decree to punish eternal death looks to final hardness as meritorious cause; decree not to free him by special mercy cannot look to foreseen unbelief as motive
latin: Quod Deus ab omni aeternitate decreverit Judam aeterna morte punire, id decretum respicit finalem Judae in peccatis suis obdurationem, tanquam causam ejusdem supplicii-decreti motivam et meritoriam: Sed quod Deus ab omni aeternitate decreverit non liberare Judam e statu miseriae et peccati per specialem misericordiam, sicuti decrevit liberare Paulum et Petrum; quod decreverit non emollire cor Judae, sed permittere ut obduresceret finaliter in impoenitentia et infidelitate sua—hoc decretum non potest referri ad praevisam Judae infidelitatem, tanquam causam motivam, quia nullum malum Deo praevidetur tanquam certo et absolute futurum nisi praemisso et praesupposito decreto Dei de permissione ejusdem.
pass_a: That God from all eternity decreed to punish Judas with everlasting death, that decree looks unto Judas’s final hardness in his sins, as the motive and meritorious cause of the same decree of torment: But that God from all eternity decreed not to free Judas from the state of misery and sin by special mercy, just as he decreed to free Paul and Peter; that he decreed not to soften Judas’s heart, but to permit that he should finally harden in his impenitence and unbelief—this decree cannot be referred unto Judas’s foreseen unbelief as a motive cause, because no evil is foreseen unto God as certainly and absolutely future unless God’s decree of permitting the same has been premised and presupposed.
pass_b: That God from eternity decreed to punish Judas with everlasting death looks to Judas’s final hardness in his sins as that torment-decree’s motive and meritorious cause. But that from eternity he decreed not to free Judas from misery and sin by special mercy—as he decreed to free Paul and Peter—and not to soften Judas’s heart, but to permit final hardening in impenitence and unbelief: that decree cannot be referred to Judas’s foreseen unbelief as its motive, because no evil is foreseen to God as certainly and absolutely future unless his decree to permit it is already premised and presupposed.

lemmas.lemma: non liberare Judam ... non potest referri ad praevisam

title: Cap. X Arg. IX close: the decree to permit final hardness is reprobation itself — Rom. ix. 18; futile to refer non-preparing soft-heart grace to foreseen unbelief
latin: At hoc ipsum decretum quo Deus statuit apud se velle permittere, ut quis obdurescat et extremum diem claudat in sua impoenitentia et infidelitate, est ipsissimum reprobationis decretum. Frustra igitur hac in re ad praevisam infidelitatem refertur voluntas Dei non praeparantis huic aut illi singulari personae gratiam illam quae cor emollit, quae fidem, resipiscentiam, et perseverantiam gignit, cum hic necessario confugiendum sit ad illud Apostoli, Deus cujus vult miseretur, et quem vult indurat, Rom. ix. 18.
pass_a: But this very decree by which God has established with himself to will to permit that someone harden and close his last day in his impenitence and unbelief, is the very decree of reprobation itself. In vain therefore in this matter is God’s will of not preparing for this or that singular person that grace which softens the heart, which begets faith, repentance, and perseverance, referred unto foreseen unbelief, since here one must of necessity flee unto that of the Apostle, God has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens, Rom. ix. 18.
pass_b: But the very decree by which God settles with himself to permit someone to harden and close his last day in impenitence and unbelief is reprobation’s own decree. So it is futile here to refer to foreseen unbelief God’s will not to prepare for this or that singular person the grace that softens the heart and begets faith, repentance, and perseverance—for here one must flee to the Apostle (Rom. ix. 18): God has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens.

title: Cap. X Arg. X open: if after sufficient grace election arose from foresight, the divide would be man’s act under indifferent grace—not a gift prepared for one and not the other
latin: Si post administratam sufficientem gratiam electio et reprobatio hominum oriretur ex praevisa horum fide, illorum infidelitate, tum discretio electorum et reprobatorum inciperet, non per aliquod uni praeparatum et donatum quod non est praeparatum et donatum alteri, sed per aliquem actum auxilio gratiae indifferenter administratae ab uno praestitum, ab altero non praestitum. At hoc nullo modo admittendum est, nisi gloriam electionis nostrae a pura Dei misericordia ad liberi arbitrii laudem velimus transferre.
pass_a: If after sufficient grace administered the election and reprobation of men arose from foresight of these men’s faith, of those men’s unbelief, then the discrimination of elect and reprobate would begin, not through something prepared and given unto one which is not prepared and given unto the other, but through some act under the help of grace indifferently administered, performed by one, not performed by the other. But this is by no means to be admitted, unless we will to transfer the glory of our election from the pure mercy of God unto the praise of free will.
pass_b: If after sufficient grace is administered, men’s election and reprobation arose from foresight of these men’s faith and those men’s unbelief, then the divide of elect and reprobate would begin not by something prepared and given to one and not to the other, but by an act one performs and another does not under help from grace given indifferently. That must not be admitted unless we mean to shift the glory of our election from God’s pure mercy to the praise of free will.

lemmas.gloss: foresight scheme: divide = human act under common grace

lemmas.lemma: gloriam electionis ... ad liberi arbitrii laudem
lemmas.gloss: would transfer election’s glory to free will

title: Cap. X Arg. X: adversaries put Peter and Judas under the same sufficient grace — free-will use separates them; that contradicts 1 Cor. iv. 7 Quis te discernit?
latin: De consequentia dubitari non potest, quia ex sententia adversariorum, administrata tam Judae quam Petro gratia sufficiente ad credendum et resipiscendum, bonus usus liberi arbitrii amplectentis hanc gratiam sufficientem utrique communiter oblatam posuit Petrum in numero credentium et electorum, et malus usus liberi arbitrii repellentis eandem arcuit Judam a numero credentium et electorum. Sed hoc e diametro adversatur sententiae illi Paulinae 1 Cor. iv. 7, Quis te discernit? quid habes quod non acceperis? quod si accepisti, quid gloriaris ut qui non acceperis?
pass_a: Concerning the consequence there can be no doubt, because from the adversaries’ sentence, sufficient grace unto believing and repenting having been administered both unto Judas and unto Peter, the good use of free will embracing this sufficient grace commonly offered unto both placed Peter in the number of believers and elect, and the bad use of free will thrusting back the same shut Judas out from the number of believers and elect. But this diametrically opposes that Pauline sentence 1 Cor. iv. 7, Who discerns thee? what hast thou which thou didst not receive? and if thou didst receive, why dost thou glory as if thou didst not receive?
pass_b: The consequence cannot be doubted. On the adversaries’ view, with sufficient grace to believe and repent administered to Judas and Peter alike, free will’s good use embracing that common offer put Peter among believers and elect, and free will’s bad use thrusting it back shut Judas out. That stands diametrically against Paul’s word (1 Cor. iv. 7): Who makes you to differ? What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why boast as though you did not?

lemmas.gloss: same sufficient grace to Judas and Peter
1 Cor. iv.7 who makes you differ
